subject: Cooking
title: Curing: Salt as a Preservative
description: Learn Curing: Salt as a Preservative in one minute.

hook.text: Before refrigerators, sailors survived on salt pork that lasted months at sea. Salt saved lives.

buildup.text: Salt draws water out of food through osmosis, creating an environment too dry for most bacteria.

discovery.text: At 10%+ salt concentration, most harmful bacteria simply cannot survive or reproduce.

twist.text: Curing also uses nitrates, which prevent botulism — the most dangerous food-borne toxin known.

climax.text: Prosciutto is just pork leg and salt, aged 12–36 months. No cooking required — salt does the work.

punchline.text: Salt doesn't just season. It defends against death.

quiz.question: How does salt primarily preserve food?
options: Removes water bacteria need to survive

details.summary: Salt curing preserves food by drawing out moisture through osmosis and creating an environment too hostile for most bacteria. Curing salt with sodium nitrite adds color preservation and prevents botulism in products like bacon, ham, and salami.
details.whyItMatters: Curing is one of humanity's oldest food preservation techniques. Understanding the science behind it explains how traditional charcuterie works and why safety rules matter.
takeaways: Salt dehydrates food and inhibits bacterial growth through osmosis
Sodium nitrite in curing salt prevents deadly botulism toxin
Proper salt concentration is critical for safe preservation

faq.question: What is the difference between curing salt and table salt?
faq.answer: Curing salt contains sodium nitrite mixed with regular salt, dyed pink to prevent confusion. Sodium nitrite inhibits botulism bacteria and preserves the pink color of cured meats. Regular table salt preserves through dehydration alone but does not prevent botulism in anaerobic environments.

faq.question: Is sodium nitrite in cured meats dangerous?
faq.answer: At regulated levels, sodium nitrite is safe and prevents fatal botulism. High-heat cooking can convert nitrites to nitrosamines, which are concerning. Cured meats contain far less nitrite than many vegetables naturally do, but moderation is still recommended.
